title: How Willpower Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss willpower: how it is defined, the Freudian ego and finite energy idea, Roy Baumeister's ego depletion experiments (radishes vs. chocolate, persistence puzzles), Baba Shiv's working memory study, fMRI findings on prefrontal cortex activity, glucose as a willpower booster, the Israeli parole board study, decision fatigue and its effect on the poor, the marshmallow experiment and a University of Rochester follow-up, and genetic influences. The episode also covers site announcements and a listener mail from Todd in Oklahoma City.
topics: John Tierney New York Times decision fatigue

entities.name: Do You Suffer from Decision Fatigue?

segments.title: Opening banter and site announcements
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, mention the new website, Twitter, and Facebook, then introduce willpower as a shared struggle.

segments.title: Defining willpower and the higher self vs. lower self
segments.summary: The hosts connect Plato's higher self and lower self idea to willpower, and discuss how Robert Lamb's article describes humans being at odds with evolved instincts such as craving sugar and sex versus modern society.

segments.title: How willpower depends on how you view the world
segments.summary: The hosts argue that how often people exercise willpower depends on whether they see the world as full of temptations, or as something they can handle, and that willpower is a decision-making act.

segments.title: Willpower as a depletable resource and Freud's ego
segments.summary: Willpower is described as a meter that depletes and replenishes. Freud linked willpower to a finite ego energy reserve, an idea that later fell out of fashion before being revived.

segments.title: Baumeister's radish and chocolate experiments
segments.summary: Roy Baumeister at Florida State University found that people who resisted cookies and ate radishes instead had more trouble completing a persistence puzzle, suggesting willpower was used up.

segments.title: Baba Shiv's working memory study and brain imaging
segments.summary: Baba Shiv at the University of Iowa found that people holding a seven-digit number resisted chocolate cake less well than those holding a two-digit number, linking working memory to self-control. Brain scans showed the anterior and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activity during good decisions.

segments.title: Muscle analogy, personal anecdote, and glucose
segments.summary: Baumeister compares willpower to a muscle. Chuck describes choosing to walk upstairs for a mail key as a willpower exercise. The hosts then discuss glucose research showing a sugar shot can restore willpower, initially dismissed by other scientists and later supported by brain imaging.

segments.title: Israeli parole board, decision fatigue, and poverty
segments.summary: A study of an Israeli parole board found parole chances dropped the longer since a break, with decision fatigue leading to risk-averse denials. The hosts discuss how decision fatigue may disproportionately affect poor people.

segments.title: Rush lyric, free will, and the marshmallow experiments
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Rush's free will lyric about choosing not to decide. They then describe the 1960s marshmallow experiment, where children who waited had better later SAT outcomes, and a University of Rochester follow-up showing children who had been promised art supplies waited longer when the promise was kept.

segments.title: Listener mail from Todd in Oklahoma City
segments.summary: Todd writes that the podcast helped him impress his girlfriend with interesting facts. The hosts thank him and invite feedback via Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode, inviting listeners to visit the website and sign off.
